query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying ultrasonic surface rolling processing (USRP) pre-treatment followed by plasma nitriding at 850 °C increases the surface hardness and wear resistance of titanium alloys by forming a thicker, harder titanium nitride layer with enhanced surface topography.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated titanium alloy with its native oxide surface, exhibiting relatively low hardness and poor abrasive wear resistance.
generation.intervention: First, subject the titanium alloy to USRP pre-treatment to induce surface densification and microtexturing, and then perform plasma nitriding at 850 °C to facilitate deep and uniform nitride layer formation.
generation.conditions: The hypothesis is expected to hold under abrasive wear test conditions (e.g., using simulated abrasive particles such as simulated lunar regolith or standardized abrasive media) at ambient temperature and moderate load settings.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a significantly thicker and harder titanium nitride layer combined with a dimpled surface morphology (from USRP) that can trap wear debris.
generation.mechanism: USRP pre-treatment refines the surface microstructure and creates beneficial micro-dimples that serve as nucleation sites for nitriding, thereby promoting a uniform and deeper penetration of nitrogen during plasma nitriding. The enhanced nitride layer increases hardness and offers improved resistance to abrasive wear by reducing material removal during micro-cutting or fatigue wear processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated titanium alloys will exhibit at least a 50% increase in surface hardness and a correspondingly lower wear rate compared to untreated alloys under identical testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated titanium alloy subjected to the same abrasive wear testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The anticipated improvements are expected under standard ambient conditions and moderate loads; extreme operating temperatures or very high loads might reduce the effectiveness of the nitride layer, thereby limiting the intervention's benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal parameters for both USRP and plasma nitriding (e.g., duration, temperature, and related process variables) may require further tuning, and the effectiveness might differ depending on the specific titanium alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of titanium alloy specimens: one group undergoes USRP pre-treatment followed by plasma nitriding at 850 °C, and the other group is left untreated. Expose both groups to abrasive wear conditions using standardized abrasive particles or simulated lunar regolith in a controlled tribological test setup. Measure and compare the surface hardness, wear rate, nitride layer thickness, and surface topography between the two groups.
measurements: Surface hardness (using microindentation tests such as Vickers or Knoop hardness measurements)
Wear rate (by measuring mass or volume loss after a fixed number of cycles)
Nitride layer thickness (using cross-sectional metallography or SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 50% higher hardness and a corresponding reduction in wear rate with p<0.05) compared to the untreated specimens, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
The objective of the given work was to investigate abrasive wear behaviours of titanium (Ti) treated by ultrasonic surface rolling processing (USRP) pre-treatment and plasma nitriding (PN). Simulated lunar regolith particles (SLRPs) were employed as abrasive materials during characterization of tribological performances. The experimental results showed that SLRPs cause severe abrasive wear on Ti plasma-nitrided at 750 °C via the mechanism of micro-cutting. Due to the formation of a harder and thicker nitriding layer, the abrasive wear resistance of the Ti plasma-nitrided at 850 °C was enhanced, and its wear mechanism was mainly fatigue. USRP pre-treatment was effective at enhancing the abrasive wear resistance of plasma-nitrided Ti, due to the enhancement of the hardness and thickness of the nitride layer. Nevertheless, SLRPs significantly decreased the friction coefficient of Ti treated by USRP pre-treatment and PN, because the rolling of small granular abrasives impeded the adhesion of the worn surface. ## Abstract
AbstractThe study assessed the effect of ion nitriding on the properties of the surface layer of Grade 5 titanium alloy used, among others, in medicine. Titanium and its alloys have low hardness and insufficient wear resistance in conditions of friction which limits the use of these materials. The improvement of these properties is only possible by the appropriate modification of the surface layer of these alloys. The ion nitriding process was carried out in a wide temperature range, i.e., 530–590 °C, and in the time range 5–17 h. Two variants of nitriding were applied: cathodic (conventional) nitriding and nitriding using the active screen method. The research results presented in this article allow for stating that each of the applied nitriding variants improves the analysed properties (nitrogen diffusion depth, hardness, wear resistance, microstructure analysis and surface topography) of the surface layers in relation to the material before nitriding. The hardness increased in every nitriding variant (the use of the additional active screen increased the hardness to 1021 HK0.025).
